editorNote: A New Mexico court's $567 million ruling against Meta and AMD's acquisition of silicon-etching chip startup Taalas both point the same direction: consequences for AI-era business decisions are landing for real, not hypothetically. OpenAI narrowed the gap between its free and paid tiers, Qwen3.8-Max's benchmark gains came with a spike in hallucinations, and a browser-game study quantified just how bad humans are at catching malicious AI-agent commands. One essay closes the issue: with production nearly free, taste — not output — is the scarce skill left.

stories.headline: New Mexico court orders Meta to pay $567 million over harms to children's mental health
stories.summary: A judge in New Mexico ordered Meta to pay $567 million into a fund for youth mental health treatment and prevention programs, with $420 million earmarked for treatment services over the next five years. The ruling is the second phase of a trial Meta lost in March, when jurors separately ordered $375 million in civil penalties after finding the company knowingly harmed children's mental health and concealed what it knew about child sexual exploitation on its platforms.
stories.whyItMatters: Combined with March's penalty, Meta's total liability in the case reaches $942 million, and the judge also ordered platform changes including AI-based age-verification tools; Meta says it will appeal.

sourceLinks.title: Meta ordered to pay $567 million into abatement fund as remedy to child harms case in New Mexico

stories.headline: AMD acquires AI chip startup Taalas to etch model weights directly into silicon
stories.summary: AMD has acquired Toronto-based Taalas, which builds model-specific chips that embed AI model weights directly into silicon instead of relying on external memory; terms were not disclosed. Taalas's HC1 chip has demonstrated 16,960 tokens per second running Meta's Llama 3.1 8B model, about 48x faster than competing GPU setups, though each chip is locked to the specific model it was manufactured for.
stories.whyItMatters: AMD plans to pair the technology with its Helios rack systems for high-speed token generation, directly targeting Nvidia's inference business for AI agents and code assistants.

sourceLinks.title: AMD acquires AI chip startup Taalas to boost inference performance by etching models into silicon

stories.headline: OpenAI tightens GPT-5.6 Sol's responses and gives free ChatGPT users unlimited Luna access
stories.summary: OpenAI updated GPT-5.6 Sol for paying subscribers to give more focused answers, cut unnecessary detail, and added a slider to control reasoning depth per response. Free and Go users are getting GPT-5.6 Luna as their default model with unlimited text chats and a new Think button, though they lose access to Sol entirely. OpenAI's internal testing found responses with at least one factual error fell about 62% for Luna and 68% for Sol compared with the prior GPT-5.5 Instant.
stories.whyItMatters: The changes formalize a two-tier product split — a leaner free model versus a more capable paid one — while OpenAI's own accuracy claims remain internally sourced and unverified.

sourceLinks.title: OpenAI improves GPT-5.6 Sol in ChatGPT and restricts free users to its weakest model

stories.headline: Qwen3.8-Max climbs the agentic benchmarks but its hallucination rate nearly doubles
stories.summary: Alibaba's Qwen3.8-Max scored 56 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index — level with Claude Opus 4.8 and ahead of every Google, Meta, and xAI model, trailing only Anthropic, OpenAI, and Moonshot's Kimi K3. On GDPval-AA it reached 1739 Elo, a 468-point jump over its predecessor, taking an average of 64 turns to complete tasks versus 14 for Qwen3.7 Max. But on the AA-Omniscience evaluation, its hallucination rate climbed from 23% to 40% as the model attempted more questions it previously would have declined to answer.
stories.whyItMatters: The trade-off shows Qwen3.8-Max's benchmark gains came partly from a willingness to guess rather than abstain, a design choice that inflates wrong answers alongside right ones.

sourceLinks.title: Qwen 3.8 Max Scores 56 On Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, Ahead Of All US Companies Except Anthropic And OpenAI

stories.headline: Study: humans miss 1 in 3 malicious commands when supervising AI agents
stories.summary: An interactive browser game testing human-in-the-loop approval of AI agent commands, spanning more than 40,000 runs and roughly 409,000 individual decisions, found players caught threats with only 66.3% accuracy. Credential-exfiltration attempts were missed 35% of the time, and one disguised command, npm run analyze, was approved 64.7% of the time despite containing a malicious payload; only 20.8% of players caught every threat.
stories.whyItMatters: The results suggest permission fatigue undermines human oversight as a safety backstop for autonomous AI agents — the more approvals a person reviews, the less scrutiny each one gets.

sourceLinks.title: Humans missed 1 in 3 threats approving AI agent commands across 40k game runs

stories.headline: Essay: with AI making production nearly free, taste is the only scarce skill left
stories.summary: The essay argues that as AI tools remove the friction of building software, the human judgment to distinguish what's worth making from what merely works — taste — has become the scarce resource, since production itself is no longer rationed by cost or effort. It frames taste as compressed judgment built through past mistakes, and warns that near-zero production costs flood the field with competent-but-mediocre output, making curation rather than creation the remaining craft.
stories.whyItMatters: The argument reframes the value of AI coding tools: they collapse the cost of output but do nothing to solve the harder problem of deciding which output deserves to exist.
